ShareCommentary: Code review is not a gate, it's a conversation. When my team started treating reviews as 'approve or block', cycle time went up and trust went down. We changed one thing: every review must start with what the author did well and one question before any request. Within a month, median review time dropped from 26 hours to 9, and people started asking for reviews earlier instead of hiding big pull requests.

The best on-call rotation I ever ran had a rule: if you get paged twice for the same thing, fixing it becomes the top priority for the next sprint. Not a ticket in the backlog. The top priority. Pages are a tax your past self charges your future self, and someone has to stop paying it.

I've interviewed over 200 engineers. The signal I trust most isn't the algorithm question. It's how someone talks about a bug they caused. People who can describe their own mistake calmly, with what they learned and what they changed, tend to be the ones who make teams safer.

Hot take: most 'platform teams' fail because they build what's interesting, not what's adopted. My test for any internal tool: would a team choose it if it were optional? If the answer is no, you're not building a platform, you're building a mandate.

Writing a design doc is not about the doc. It's about finding the disagreement early, when it's cheap. My template has one section people skip and shouldn't: 'What would make this the wrong decision?' Fill that in honestly and half your review meeting is already done.

New managers often ask me how to run 1:1s. Mine have three questions that never change: What's on your mind? What's getting in your way? What do you want to be doing more of in six months? The third one is where careers actually get shaped.

We cut our deploy time from 40 minutes to 6. The biggest win wasn't caching or parallel tests. It was deleting 300 tests that had not failed in two years and tested nothing anyone cared about. Every test is a promise you keep paying for. Audit your promises.

AI coding tools changed how my team works, but not in the way I expected. The engineers who benefit most are the ones who already write clear tickets and small pull requests. AI amplifies your habits. If your habits are messy, you just get mess faster.
Thanks everyone for the kind messages!
